diagnostic_evidence.quote: A countable family $\{\varphi_j\}_{j=1}^{\infty} \subset L^{2}(P_X)$ is \emph{complete} in $L^{2}(P_X)$ if its linear span is dense in $L^{2}(P_X)$
In most examples one may take $\X \subseteq \R^{d}$ and $\Y \subseteq \R^{k}$, although the same notation also covers image-valued or function-valued outputs

issues.failure_explanation: The sentence asserts that polynomial, Fourier, and wavelet bases are complete in L^2(P_X) with no hypothesis on P_X, hedging only the radial-basis case. For a general law on R^d this is false: the polynomial span is dense in L^2(P_X) only under additional conditions such as compact support or determinacy of the moment problem; for moment-indeterminate laws (e.g. lognormal-type P_X) polynomials are not dense in L^2(P_X), and for heavy-tailed P_X the monomials need not even belong to L^2(P_X), violating Definition def:complete's own requirement that the family be a subset of L^2(P_X). Trigonometric (Fourier) families additionally require P_X to be supported on a bounded torus-like domain. The claim is stated for the general P_X fixed in Section 2.

failure_location.quote: Polynomial bases, Fourier bases, wavelet bases, and---under additional hypotheses on $P_X$---Gaussian or sigmoidal radial basis functions are complete

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the missing hypotheses to the sentence, e.g. 'for compactly supported (or moment-determinate) P_X, polynomial and trigonometric/wavelet families are complete', mirroring the hedge already given for radial basis functions.
issues.overall_effect: The justification that classical rich feature families can approximate the conditional mean arbitrarily well is overstated in generality. No labelled theorem and none of the paper's examples (all with compactly supported or effectively bounded X) rely on the unhedged version, so nothing downstream fails.
issues.title: Unqualified completeness claim for polynomial/Fourier/wavelet bases in L^2(P_X)
issues.why_classification: A standard local hypothesis (compact support / moment determinacy) restores a true statement; the method, all theorems, rates, and all examples are unaffected.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: On the \(n=2000\) diagnostic samples we evaluate the significance \(t_n(\psi)\) and the effect size \(e_n(\psi)\)
taking \(\psi\) to be the orthonormalized Legendre probes \(\sqrt{2k+1}\,P_k\); the factor \(\sqrt{2k+1}\) gives unit variance under \(X\sim\mathrm{Unif}[-1,1]\)

issues.failure_explanation: From the definitions, t_n^2 = n*e_n*sigma_r^2/sigma(psi)^2 identically. For the fully specified law and the degree-2 fit (population projection Pi_2 m = -0.4775 x), the population limits on the n=2000 diagnostic set are: E[r psi] = c_5/sqrt(11) = 0.556 (so e_n -> 0.556^2/0.719 = 0.430, exactly the reported value), sigma_r^2 -> E[(m-Pi_2 m)^2] + E[a^2] = 0.424+0.295 = 0.719, and for the unit-variance probe psi = sqrt(11) P_5, sigma(psi)^2 -> E[((m-Pi_2 m)^2 + a^2) psi^2] = 0.85 > sigma_r^2, because the residual second moment is positively correlated with P_5^2 (the deterministic misfit is dominated by its 0.556*psi component, and a(x)^2 is maximal at x in {0,+/-1} where psi^2 is also large or the P_5^2 edge spike dominates). Hence the defined statistic necessarily satisfies |t_n| < sqrt(n*e_n) = sqrt(860) = 29.3 and converges to approximately 27. The reported |t_n| = 34 exceeds sqrt(n*e_n), which would require sigma(psi)^2 = 0.74*sigma_r^2 (negative correlation between residual magnitude and psi^2), contradicting the specified law. The value 34 is instead exactly the population value of T_n divided by the centered standard deviation of the products r_i psi(x_i), namely sqrt(2000)*0.556/sqrt(0.85-0.556^2) = 34.0 -- a different statistic from the one defined (the two denominators coincide only under the null, where E[r psi]=0).
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Either correct the reported value to that of the defined statistic (approximately 27), or redefine sigma(psi)^2 as the centered variance of the residual-probe products (also asymptotically standard normal under the null) and keep the reported number; either local edit restores consistency between the definitions and the reported result.
issues.overall_effect: The reported significance value of the flagship diagnostic in the controlled demonstration is not the value of the defined statistic; the definitions of Section 3.3 and the reported experimental values are mutually inconsistent. The qualitative conclusions (P_5 overwhelmingly significant; degree-2 fit in Regime I; degree-9 fit at the barrier) are unaffected, since both 27 and 34 are far above the 1.96 critical value.
issues.title: Reported |t_n| = 34 for the P_5 probe is inconsistent with the paper's own definition of the t-statistic
issues.why_classification: A single-number correction or a one-line definitional alignment repairs it; the significance verdict, the regime classification, the stop rule, and all other claims and guarantees are unchanged.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The probe family is the monomials of the standardized stencil up to total degree~6; a probe is \emph{out-of-basis} for a degree-\(p\) fit if its total degree exceeds \(p\).
For a probe standardized to zero mean and unit variance on the diagnostic set,
with the task tolerance fixed at $\varepsilon=0.01$, the same value as in Section~\ref{subsec:exp-twobranch}

issues.failure_explanation: By the definitions, e_n(psi) equals the fraction of residual variance removable by a linear correction along psi multiplied by the probe's empirical second moment (1/n) Sum_i psi(x_i)^2, since the removable fraction is (Sum r_i psi_i)^2/(Sum psi_i^2 Sum r_i^2) while e_n = (Sum r_i psi_i)^2/(n Sum r_i^2). The fraction interpretation therefore holds only for probes standardized to zero mean and unit variance, as Section 3.3 explicitly stipulates and as the two-branch experiment enforces via the orthonormalized probes sqrt(2k+1) P_k. The stated L96 probe family -- raw monomials of the standardized stencil variables -- does not satisfy this: for a standardized variable x, E[x^4] > 1 strictly (Jensen), and even higher-degree monomials have second moments far from 1. As written, the computed e_n values are thus not the claimed fractions, depend on each monomial's scale, and are not comparable to the tolerance eps = 0.01 imported from Section 6.1. Moreover, at p = 3 the reported maximum e_n = 0.0034 lies below the null level that raw monomials would produce (their second moments inflate the null level of e_n well above 1/480), so the reported values are consistent only with an unstated per-probe standardization.

failure_location.quote: For each fit we compute the effect size \(e_n(\psi)\) of \eqref{eq:effect-size} on the diagnostic snapshots---the fraction of residual variance a correction along \(\psi\) would remove.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: State that each monomial probe is standardized to zero mean and unit variance on the diagnostic set before e_n is computed (the convention the reported values evidently use); the fraction interpretation, the eps-comparison, and the p = 3 selection then all stand, the decay 0.193 -> 0.047 -> 0.0034 being robust under any fixed normalization.
issues.overall_effect: The stated meaning of the L96 effect sizes, and with it the stated basis for the eps-comparison by which the stop rule selects p = 3 (and hence the framing of the selected closure as sitting at the conditional-mean barrier), is unsupported as written; the reported magnitudes imply a normalization step the text does not specify. No labelled formal result is affected.
issues.title: L96 effect sizes on unstandardized monomial probes do not measure the claimed fraction of removable residual variance
issues.why_classification: A one-sentence specification of the probe normalization restores every claimed meaning and the selection; no theorem, rate, guarantee, or advertised scope is lost.
